tldr: The authors developed "Aero Hand Open," a tendon-driven 5-finger hand that costs only $314 in parts. By faithfully modeling the cable transmission in MuJoCo and establishing a bidirectional actuation map, they achieved zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of a policy trained entirely in simulation with no fine-tuning.
overview:
Dexterous manipulation by robotic hands has long been a challenging problem. Contact between fingertips and objects switches discretely, making the dynamics extremely complex. In addition, multi-fingered hands have presented a dual barrier: they are either prohibitively expensive or, even if affordable, difficult to use for learning. In particular, anthropomorphic tendon-driven hands are powerful because moving the actuators off the joints allows for smaller, lower-cost designs. However, because multiple joints are coupled through a single cable to form an underactuated transmission, accurately reproducing this transmission system inside a simulator has been extremely difficult.

To address this, the authors propose "Aero Hand Open," an open-source tendon-driven hand designed from scratch to be simulation-ready. It drives 16 degrees of freedom across its joints using only 7 motors, and all structural parts can be manufactured with a 3D printer. The key highlights are the faithful reproduction of the cable routing (geometric pulley paths) in MuJoCo derived directly from CAD data, and the identification of a bidirectional actuation map connecting motor commands to tendon lengths, including the complex three-way coupling of the thumb.

For validation, an in-hand continuous cube rotation task was trained using reinforcement learning. The policy uses only observations obtainable from the real hardware's encoders—without any additional sensors or state estimation—and was deployed directly to the physical hand. As a result, the policy trained entirely in simulation operated directly on the real hardware, successfully achieving stable continuous rotation at roughly 55 seconds per revolution in a zero-shot manner.
contributions: Open-sourced the mechanical design and control stack for a 5-finger hand weighing 374g with a $314 bill-of-materials cost, where all parts can be 3D-printed for easy repair, covering 33 human grasp types.
Constructed a simulation model in MuJoCo that accurately reproduces CAD-based pulley wrapping paths and faithfully captures each finger's tendon transmission and return springs.

Constructed and identified a bidirectional linear actuation map between the simulation and real motors—including the three-axis coupling of the thumb—demonstrating high-precision kinematic and dynamic tracking.
Achieved zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of an in-hand cube rotation policy trained purely in simulation, relying solely on motor encoder readings available on the physical hand as observations.

sections.heading: Why is Sim-to-Real So Difficult with Low-Cost Tendon-Driven Hands?
sections.summary: Multi-fingered hands are essential for dexterous manipulation, but conventional tendon-driven hands have been either too expensive or difficult to reproduce in simulation, making them unsuitable for learning. This work pairs a low-cost, 3D-printed hand with a faithful simulator transmission model to achieve zero-shot transfer from simulation to real hardware.
sections.details:
Dexterous manipulation with robotic hands involves frequent contact formation and breaking, which causes discontinuous dynamics. Consequently, reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation has become the dominant approach. However, this demands a simulator model that reproduces the physical properties of the hardware with extreme fidelity.

Actuation approaches for robot hands broadly fall into three categories: tendon-driven (cable-driven), direct-drive joints, and pneumatic actuation. Direct-drive hands (such as the LEAP Hand) offer ease of use because joint angles can be directly commanded and observed, but housing motors inside joints tends to make the fingers bulky, compromising human-like anthropomorphism. On the other hand, tendon-driven hands (such as the Shadow Hand) feature superior anthropomorphic structures, but commercial products have cost tens of thousands of dollars or more. While low-cost DIY hands exist, they have lacked simulation models capable of supporting learning.

Building tendon-driven hands affordably results in an underactuated structure, where a limited number of motors pull many joints. When a single cable is pulled, which joint bends first is governed by dynamic equilibrium. Cable slack, friction, and inter-joint coupling emerge, which cannot be simulated by standard joint position control models. Just as actuator-level identification was the key to zero-shot transfer in quadrupedal robots, this paper models the tendon transmission itself to build a simulation-complete learning pipeline for the $314 Aero Hand Open.

sections.heading: A $314, 374g Hardware Design: 5 Fingers and 16 Joints Built for Rapid Repair
sections.summary: Aero Hand Open features 5 fingers and 16 revolute joints, driven by just 7 serial bus servos in a lightweight 374g hand. All structural parts can be printed on an FDM 3D printer, allowing rapid in-house reprinting and repair whenever wear or breakage occurs.
sections.details:
The overarching design philosophy of the hand is centered on being "faithfully reproducible in simulation and easily repairable in the field."

### 2.1 Overview
The external dimensions are $198 \times 95 \times 53.5$ mm, with a weight of only 374g. Seven Feetech serial bus servomotors are mounted on the back of the hand (dorsum). Fifteen joints are driven by cables, while thumb abduction is directly driven by a linkage. Sensing uses a minimal, clean configuration relying solely on the motors' internal magnetic encoders (7 degrees of freedom).

### 2.2 Kinematics and Transmission
- **Four Fingers (Index to Pinky)**: Each finger has 3 joints (MCP: base, PIP: middle, DIP: distal), simultaneously actuated by a single braided Kevlar/Vectran cable. Extension is passive, driven by piano wire torsion springs. A key design element is the staged spring stiffness: the MCP spring at the base is compliant, while the distal PIP/DIP springs are stiff. When the cable is reeled in, the MCP joint bends up to 90 degrees first to press the object against the palm before the distal joints curl inward. This enables adaptive grasping that naturally conforms to object shapes with just a single cable.
- **Thumb**: The thumb has 4 joints. Its circumduction sweeping across the palm (abduction/adduction) is directly actuated by a linkage spanning 0 to 100 degrees (1.75 rad). The remaining flexion motion is controlled by 2 cables. Because these cables route across the abduction axis, abducting the thumb pulls on the flexion cables. This creates a three-axis geometric coupling, and this exact coupling provides the thumb's rich dexterity.

### 2.3 Actuation, Sensing, and Grasping Performance
Control is handled by an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, connected to a PC via a single USB-C cable alongside a 24V power supply. The encoders provide 16-bit resolution. The hand delivers approximately 12N of fingertip force and can cycle open/close at roughly 1.2 Hz. With a single hardware configuration, it is expressive enough to cover all 33 grasp types defined in the GRASP taxonomy.

### 2.4 Durability and Fabrication
The total bill of materials (BOM) is approximately $314, with the servomotors accounting for about two-thirds at $209. All structural components can be printed in PLA filament on standard 3D printers (e.g., Bambu Lab X1C) in about 13 hours. In endurance testing, the hand completed over 400,000 full open-close cycles (equivalent to over 90 hours of continuous operation) without cable breakage or range-of-motion degradation, proving sufficient durability for learning workloads.

sections.heading: Down to the Pulleys: Building a Tendon-Level Simulation in MuJoCo
sections.summary: In the MuJoCo physics simulator, 16 hinge joints, 20 spatial tendons, and 7 actuators were modeled. By directly importing the wrapping geometry of each pulley from CAD data, the hand reproduces an accurate tendon transmission without relying on arbitrary parameter tuning.
sections.details:
When matching tendon-driven behavior in a simulator, manually tuning moment arms as in traditional joint-torque models fails to capture nonlinearities that shift with posture. To solve this, this work physically routes cables using MuJoCo's "Spatial Tendon" feature.

### 3.1 Tendon Modeling via Spatial Tendons
Each of the four fingers is strung with 4 tendons: a drive cable, a PIP-DIP coupling cable, and 2 extension springs. The thumb incorporates 2 flexion cables and springs. In MuJoCo, if the side on which a spatial tendon wraps around a pulley (cylinder geometry) is not explicitly defined, the solver takes the shortest path and wraps around the wrong side, flipping the sign of the moment arm. To prevent this, pulley cylinders with radii of 1.7 to 4.5 mm (mostly 2.5 mm) were placed exactly as specified in the CAD model, explicitly fixing the wrapping side across all 24 finger pulley points. Physical spring stiffness values (e.g., 352 N/m for the MCP, 4000 N/m for distal joints) were directly input from part specifications.

### 3.2 Actuation Interface
For the 6 drive cables, position actuators directly command target tendon lengths (gain $k_p=10^4$), while the thumb abduction joint is assigned a joint position actuator ($k_p=1$) due to its direct linkage. As a result, the simulator's control inputs correspond one-to-one with the 7 motor winches on the real hand.

### 3.3 Numerical Formulations for Parallel GPU Training
To run reinforcement learning massively parallelized on GPUs at high speed, all collision meshes were replaced with geometric primitives such as spheres and capsules. Unnecessary internal self-collisions between finger parts were excluded, and a semi-implicit Euler integrator (10 ms time step) was adopted to prevent numerical instability. Furthermore, rotor inertia arising from the motor gear ratio ($n=205$), given by $J_r n^2 = 1.56 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, was analytically incorporated as joint armature, faithfully capturing the physical dynamics during sharp accelerations and decelerations.

sections.heading: Untangling Complex Thumb Coupling: Bidirectional Actuation Mapping
sections.summary: The authors derived a bidirectional transformation (actuation map) connecting tendon length commands in simulation to 16-bit motor commands on the physical hand. Beyond simple affine transformations for the fingers, the three-axis geometric coupling linking thumb abduction and flexion was formulated as a linear relationship.
sections.details:
Because the simulator operates in tendon lengths (in meters) and the physical hand operates in motor rotation angles (16-bit integer values), a bidirectional transformation is required: a forward map to convert policy outputs into motor commands, and an inverse map to convert real encoder readings into policy observations.

### 4.1 & 4.2 Linear Kinematic Model from Joints to Excursions
The relationship between joint angles $\mathbf{q}$ and cable excursions $\mathbf{d}$ can be expressed as a linear map $\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}$, where matrix entries represent effective moment arms computed from two poses in CAD.
While the finger values are independent and positive, the thumb presents an intriguing case. The thumb flexion cables pass through the proximal joint pulley on their way to the distal joints. When the proximal joint (CMC flexion) flexes, the cable winds onto the pulley and pays out slack forward. Consequently, to hold the distal posture while flexing the proximal joint, the motor must unwind cable (negative excursion), yielding the matrix's only negative coefficient ($-2.50$ mm/rad). Due to this geometric coupling, the lower limit of the thumb motor's travel is not the fully extended pose (0 degrees), but rather a negative angle ($-15.28$ degrees) where only the proximal joint is flexed.

### 4.3 Forward and Inverse Actuation Maps
For the four fingers, simple 1D affine transformations matching the full-extension and clenched-fist endpoints are sufficient. However, for the thumb, where abduction link motion alters the two flexion cable lengths, a linear map estimating joint angles was constructed via least-squares regression over a workspace sweep in simulation ($R^2 \geq 0.9995$, showing exceptional linearity). The slight geometric coupling from abduction to flexion that was missing inside the simulation model is compensated for in software within this mapping layer.

### 4.4 & 4.5 Kinematic and Dynamic Validation
- **Kinematic Validation**: Comparing cable excursions between the real hand and the model from full extension to a clenched fist revealed finger errors of only $0.04 \sim 1.40$ mm (less than 3% of the total 44.45 mm stroke), demonstrating remarkable agreement.
- **Dynamic Validation**: In dynamic tracking tests using step commands over 134 seconds, steady-state RMS tracking errors across the four fingers stayed within $0.29 \sim 0.45$ mm (0.6% to 1.0% of full scale). Although the simulator's step-response rise time was 10 to 40 ms faster, it confirmed that the physical dynamics were captured with very high fidelity.

sections.heading: Learning with Hardware-Only Signals: RL for In-Hand Cube Rotation
sections.summary: Using the identified model, an in-hand continuous cube rotation task was trained with PPO. The policy's observation space was strictly limited to real motor encoder readings and the previous action, adopting a clean formulation that assumes no external cameras or sensors.
sections.details:
Continuous in-hand cube rotation is a standard benchmark for dexterous manipulation due to the continuous cycle of making and breaking contact. This work utilized the MuJoCo Playground environment alongside Brax's PPO implementation.

### 5.1 Observation and Action Design
The key choice enabling successful real-world transfer was: "include nothing in the observation that the hardware cannot actually measure."
- **Policy (Actor) Observations (14 dimensions)**: Comprises only 7 channels of motor positions (normalized values perturbed with uniform noise) and the 7-dimensional action from the previous time step. Object pose, velocity, and fingertip contact forces are completely omitted.
- **Value Function (Critic) Privileged Information (81 dimensions)**: Adopting an asymmetric actor-critic architecture, only the critic during training receives full privileged simulator state, including 16 joint angles and velocities, actuator forces, 3D fingertip positions, and cube position, orientation, and velocity.
- **Action Space (7 dimensions)**: Outputs offsets relative to a nominal grasp posture $\boldsymbol{\ell}^0$ within $[-1, 1]$. Action scales for each channel are scaled to avoid hitting travel limits.

### 5.2 Reward Design and Domain Randomization
The reward function is remarkably simple:
$$r_t = w_\omega (\boldsymbol{\omega}_t^{\mathrm{cube}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}}) \Delta t + w_{\mathrm{fall}} \mathbbm{1}_{\mathrm{fall}} + w_a \lVert \mathbf{a}_t - \mathbf{a}_{t-1} \rVert^2$$
It contains just three terms: a reward for angular velocity around the vertical axis ($w_\omega = 1$), a penalty for dropping the cube ($w_{\mathrm{fall}} = -100$), and an action rate penalty ($w_a = -1$) to suppress abrupt setpoint changes. The action rate penalty enforces servo velocity limits and encourages smooth trajectories that the hardware can track.
To bridge the sim-to-real gap, finger link masses ($\pm 10\%$), joint damping, motor gains, and friction coefficients were randomized across parallel environments (domain randomization).

### 5.3 Training Configuration
Training was conducted across 8,192 parallel environments on a GPU for a total of $3 \times 10^8$ steps. The physics simulation runs at 100 Hz, while the control policy operates at 20 Hz.

sections.heading: Direct Sim-to-Real Transfer: Zero-Shot Cube Rotation and Error Analysis
sections.summary: Deploying the trained policy directly to the real hand as a ROS 2 node enabled stable, continuous in-hand cube rotation without fine-tuning. The real hand completed one revolution in about 55 seconds, and open-loop replay experiments isolated the residual sim-to-real discrepancy primarily to the thumb transmission.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Performance in Simulation
The learned policy smoothly and continuously rotates the cube around the vertical axis without dropping it. In simulation evaluation, it achieved 7.64 radians of rotation (about 1.22 revolutions, average angular velocity of 0.51 rad/s) within a 15-second episode.

### 6.2 Zero-Shot Real Deployment
The trained neural network was integrated into a ROS 2 node and deployed to the physical hand. No additional fine-tuning or real-world reinforcement learning was performed. The node reads motor encoders at 20 Hz, feeds them into the policy via the inverse map, and converts the resulting target cable lengths into motor commands via the forward map to drive the servos.
Even without external cameras estimating cube pose, the physical hand rotated a 50 mm, 69.2 g cube continuously without dropping it, completing a full revolution in about 55 seconds. The only adjustments made between simulation and reality were closing the nominal grasp pose by a few millimeters as a safety margin and widening action scales by 20–30%.

### 6.3 Sim-to-Real Discrepancy Analysis
To investigate why real-world rotation was slower than in simulation, an open-loop replay experiment was conducted by playing back recorded simulation actions on both the real hand and the simulator without policy feedback. While tracking error for the four fingers remained under 1 mm, the thumb's two cables exhibited substantial tracking residuals. This demonstrates that the primary remaining sim-to-real gap stems not from policy feedback dynamics, but from modeling errors in the thumb's transmission where geometric coupling was not fully captured in the simulator.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook: Accessible Learning Platforms for Tendon-Driven Hands
sections.summary: By combining a low-cost, durable, and easily repairable tendon-driven hand with a faithful transmission simulation model and bidirectional mapping, this work overcomes the sim-to-real barrier for tendon-driven hands. The entire platform—from hardware to training code—is released as open source.
sections.details:
The primary achievement of Aero Hand Open is overturning the conventional belief that low-cost tendon-driven hands cannot be used for learning due to simulation mismatches.

Rather than relying on manual moment-arm tuning, importing CAD-derived pulley routing geometry directly into MuJoCo yielded highly accurate kinematic predictions, with finger errors between 0.04 and 1.40 mm. Furthermore, designing an observation space restricted entirely to native hardware signals (7 encoders) established a robust pipeline capable of zero-shot sim-to-real transfer via pure mapping transformations, eliminating the need for state estimators.

Moving forward, the authors plan to expand the learning environment beyond in-hand cube rotation to diverse everyday tool manipulation tasks leveraging the hand's 33 grasp types. CAD files, firmware, ROS 2 nodes, MuJoCo models, and training scripts are all openly available in their repository, providing a platform anyone can replicate and build upon.

takeaways: Even with an inexpensive, underactuated tendon-driven hand, faithfully reproducing CAD-based pulley routing geometry in a simulator (MuJoCo) enables highly accurate simulation of physical transmission characteristics.
Complex multi-axis mechanisms like the thumb can be formulated and identified as linear maps through geometric analysis, creating a computationally lightweight bidirectional sim-to-real interface.

Excluding unmeasurable privileged information (object pose, contact forces) entirely from the actor's observations and relying solely on motor encoders enables robust zero-shot transfer without state estimators.

Conducting open-loop trajectory replay experiments allows researchers to cleanly isolate whether sim-to-real performance degradation originates from closed-loop policy feedback or mechanical transmission modeling errors.
limitations: The coupling effect of thumb abduction on flexion cables is not fully reproduced inside the simulator, leaving residual tracking errors of up to ~7% on the real thumb channels despite software map compensation.

Real-world cube rotation is significantly slower (~55 seconds/revolution) than in simulation (~12 seconds/revolution), indicating that dynamic properties and contact friction are not yet perfectly matched.

Because the fingertips and palm lack tactile sensors, advanced feedback control that immediately adapts contact pressure against external disturbances or unexpected object slippage remains future work.
